name: Lena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Lena, and thanks for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a grid connection crew, so we build the lines that link new solar and wind farms out on the plains to the main network. A normal day is an hour's drive out, then setting poles, stringing conductor, which is just the wire, and a lot of standing around while the senior guys argue about sag tables. I'm a first-year apprentice at 43, which is funny, because two years ago I was on an IT helpdesk telling people to restart their computers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you switch, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was going grey under fluorescent lights and I wanted to build something real, and the energy transition felt like the place to be. It's hard, I'm the weakest climber on the crew and I failed my first pole-top rescue test, which was humiliating. But I love it, and I use AI every day to make flashcards for my theory and to turn the foreman's scrawled job notes into checklists, which the guys tease me about and then ask me to do for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, which a lot of us in IT knew. But I'd also say the small stuff is still useful, I'm not giving up my flashcards. Online I'd probably write a little post saying the hype crowd owes everyone an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much for me, which is fine. The grid still needs building whatever happens with AI, all those solar farms need connecting. I'd just have more time to get better at climbing without wondering if a robot will beat me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the apprenticeship and keep using the tools in the small ways I do now. I'd probably push the union to get the company to buy a proper AI scheduling tool for the crew, because the foreman's spreadsheet is a crime. We'd keep saving the usual amount, Jonas and I have about four months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed if anything. I like the shiny stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push the union for an AI tool. Is that usual for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not usual for a union member, no. But I think we should be the ones asking for the tools, on our terms, instead of waiting for management to buy something that watches us. Better to shape it than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My climbing, honestly. I need to pass the rescue test next month or I get held back a year. That's the real thing keeping me up, not robots.

S0.say: It was oversold, which a lot of us in IT already knew, but the small stuff is still useful. I'd write a post saying the hype crowd owes everyone an apology.
S0.think: It means nothing much for me, because the grid still needs building and all those solar farms still need connecting. I'd just get time to improve my climbing without a robot racing me.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and her daily use of AI for study and checklists. Pushes the union to get the company to buy a proper scheduling tool on workers' terms, and keeps saving at the usual rate with about four months already put by.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly disappointed, because she likes new technology.
S0.quote: I'd probably push the union to get the company to buy a proper AI scheduling tool for the crew, because the foreman's spreadsheet is a crime.
S0.fieldNote: Unusual mix: a strong union supporter who wants workers to ask for AI tools rather than resist them. Her real worry right now is her pole-top rescue test, not technology. Her IT background makes her both sceptical of hype and comfortable with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why workers need a seat at the table when the tech comes in. I'd be the one at the union meeting saying, let's write the rules on drones and planning software ourselves. Online I'd share how my crew already uses these tools, the good and the bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly good. The parts of linework that robots and AI will take first are inspections, paperwork, planning, and those are things I'm actually good at from IT. Where I'm weak is climbing, and that's the bit that stays human the longest, which is ironic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my drone pilot licence, the company pays for it if you ask, and I'd ask the first week. I'd volunteer for any pilot project with the new tools. And I'd keep pushing my union branch to set up a small tech committee, I'd chair it if nobody else wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It feels like the world moving toward the bits I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henrik, who's been doing patrols by truck for thirty years and knows every pole by name. If drones take patrols, he's the one who loses the thing he's proud of. I'd want the union to find him a role teaching us, because the drones don't know what he knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but you're also junior and still learning. Is there a gap there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. I'm excited because I can see a place for myself, but I'm also the one with the least seniority, and when they reorganise, seniority still counts. I'm betting the new skills count more, and I could be wrong.

S1.say: This is exactly why workers need a seat at the table when the tech comes in. We should write the rules on drones and planning software ourselves.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good, because inspections, paperwork and planning go first and I'm good at those from IT. The climbing, where I'm weak, stays human longest, which is ironic.
S1.do: Asks in the first week for company-paid drone pilot training and volunteers for every pilot project with the new tools. Sets up and offers to chair a tech committee in her union branch.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, as the work shifts toward what she is good at.
S1.quote: Where I'm weak is climbing, and that's the bit that stays human the longest, which is ironic.
S1.fieldNote: She reads this picture as moving the job toward her strengths, while admitting her low seniority could undercut that. She keeps the union at the centre but wants it shaping the tools, not blocking them. Her concern for Henrik, an older patroller, showed she sees who loses out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any democracy to handle, and that it should be slowed down by law until there's a plan. I'd be calling for a public stake in the companies building it, so the gains don't all go to five people. I'd be posting a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even I'm not sure where I fit. I like the tools, but two years until they can do everything, including climbing, means my drone licence is worth about six months. I'd be someone who adapted fast in a world that adapted faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get the drone and robot supervision training immediately, because the first year after it arrives someone still has to watch the machines. We'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep cash instead, and I'd look hard at moving into the company's control room, where the grid is run. And I'd be in the union campaign for a public dividend every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A sort of buzzing, like too much coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what's the first thing you'd change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the long apprenticeship and think about the next two years only. Grab every skill that touches the machines, save cash, keep options. It's like a storm warning, you don't rewire the house, you get the torch and the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia, who's 13?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's okay not to know what job she'll have, because nobody does. I'd tell her to stay curious and kind, which sounds soppy, but those were the things that got me through switching careers. And I'd tell her we'll be okay, because Jonas and I are a good team.

S2.say: This is too fast for any democracy to handle, and it should be slowed by law until there's a plan. We need a public stake in the companies building it so the gains don't all go to a handful of people.
S2.think: Even I'm not sure where I fit, because two years until it can climb poles too makes my drone licence worth about six months. I'd be someone who adapted fast in a world that adapted faster.
S2.do: Takes drone and robot supervision training at once and asks about moving into the company's grid control room. Stops extra mortgage payments to hold cash instead, and campaigns weekly with her union for a public dividend.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a buzzing feeling like too much coffee.
S2.quote: I'd be someone who adapted fast in a world that adapted faster.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptive person can feel outrun, and she says so plainly. Her instinct is still to move toward the machines, but she treats it as buying a year or two rather than a career. Her politics are about public ownership of the gains, not stopping the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if we start now, and I'd say it everywhere. Public training, worker seats on company boards, a share of the gains. I'd probably end up on a panel at the union conference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me more than most people. I'd finish my ticket, get my drone and controls certificates, and be one of the people who knows both the poles and the machines. It's not safe, nothing is, but I'd be useful for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship in the first two years, then move toward the control room or the robot supervision side in years three and four. I'd keep using AI daily, obviously, and start learning how the line robots are programmed. We'd keep saving steady and maybe help Jonas get into electric bus repair, because his diesel work won't last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I feel like I've got a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonas's work. How does that shape your planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the bigger worry, honestly. He's a brilliant diesel mechanic and he hates screens. If I'm adapting and he isn't, we're still one household with one mortgage, so I'd be nagging him gently for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our camping trips would go to the cheaper sites, and I'd sell my road bike, which I barely ride anyway. We'd keep the kids' music lessons, Paul's drums are loud but they make him happy.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do this well if we start now. I'd push for public training, worker seats on company boards and a share of the gains.
S3.think: Five years suits me better than most, because I'd finish my ticket and get my drone and controls certificates, knowing both poles and machines. It's not safe, but I'd be useful for a while.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship in two years, then moves toward the control room or robot supervision in years three and four while learning how line robots are programmed. Keeps saving steadily and helps her partner move into electric bus repair.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but she feels like she has a map.
S3.quote: If I'm adapting and he isn't, we're still one household with one mortgage, so I'd be nagging him gently for five years.
S3.fieldNote: With five years her own plan is clear, and the real worry shifts to her partner, who resists screens. That household angle is what keeps her from being calm. She keeps tying personal adaptation to a political ask for shared gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, so the question is whether we're brave enough to share it fairly. I'd want a national plan with unions in it from day one. I'd be loud, but hopeful loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53, fully qualified with maybe a few years running robots or working in grid control. I'd be one of the people who knows the old way and the new way. I don't know what happens after it fully arrives, but I'd rather face it from there than from a helpdesk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the full apprenticeship properly, then add controls and robotics certificates over the following years, one a year. I'd help set up a union training scheme so older crew like Henrik can move into teaching or oversight. And I'd start a small savings pot for Mia and Paul's training, whatever they end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but steady. Mostly I'd just be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm sprinting and probably losing. With ten I can build a career that bends with it, and help other people bend too. That's the whole difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who owns the robots. If the grid gets run by machines owned by a few companies abroad, that's not a future I want my kids in, however good my job is. That's the part I'd fight about.

S4.say: A decade is plenty, so the real question is whether we're brave enough to share it fairly. I want a national plan with unions in it from day one.
S4.think: In ten years I'd be 53, fully qualified, maybe running robots or working in grid control, knowing the old way and the new. I don't know what happens after it fully arrives, but I'd rather face it from there than from a helpdesk.
S4.do: Completes the full apprenticeship, then adds one controls or robotics certificate a year. Helps set up a union training scheme for older crew and starts a savings pot for her children's training.
S4.feel: Steady and busy, with some unease at the edges.
S4.quote: If the grid gets run by machines owned by a few companies abroad, that's not a future I want my kids in, however good my job is.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets her plan a career that bends with the change, and she wants to bring older colleagues along. Her remaining unease is about ownership and fairness rather than her own job. She is one of the few who could name a concrete yearly plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it outruns even people like me who want to keep up. What would help is training that's free and fast and open to people mid-career, and a public share in the companies so the money from the robots comes back to the towns where the work used to be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about partners. Everyone talks about one worker, but I'm half of a household, and Jonas and I could adapt at totally different speeds. That's where families actually crack.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about one worker, but I'm half of a household, and Jonas and I could adapt at totally different speeds.
portrait: Lena Wagner is a 43-year-old first-year lineworker apprentice on a grid connection crew linking solar and wind farms to the network, after a career on an IT helpdesk. She lives with her partner Jonas, a diesel bus mechanic, and two children, with a mortgage and about four months of savings. She is a progressive union member who uses AI every day and wants workers to shape new tools rather than block them. She stays calm through a plateau and steady change, which she thinks favour her skills, but gets anxious at AGI in two years because it would outrun even her. With more warning her worries shift to her partner's slower adaptation and to who owns the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would outrun even people like her who want to keep up.
whatWouldHelp: Free, fast training open to mid-career workers, and a public share in the companies so the money from robots returns to the towns that lost the work.
